Netherlands $373M (2021) to $41M (2022) to a reported zero row from 2023; Germany $108M to $18M to under $0.1M; USA $55M to $10M to under $1M. sections.text: Governments name companies. Banks, exporters, shippers and insurers do the actual stopping. Evaders work in the gap between the two. This page explains the machine, the tricks, and how they can be tracked in real trade data. Trace the Unseen climate build day, 25 September 2026. Companies are named only where an official list names them.
sections.title: A sanctions list is a signal, not a wall.

sections.text: 1 · The machine A sanction is a government rule that says: do not do business with a named person, company or country. It is a way to put pressure on someone without firing a shot.
sections.title: How sanctions work

sections.text: Worldwide UN Security Council Can require every UN member to freeze assets, ban travel and embargo arms. Most often it targets named people and groups. United States Treasury (OFAC) The Office of Foreign Assets Control keeps the SDN list (the main US blacklist). Anyone on it is cut off from US dollars and US firms. United States Commerce (BIS) The Bureau of Industry and Security runs export controls. Its Entity List means: you need a licence to send US-controlled goods to this company, or even to this address. UK and EU OFSI and the EU Council The UK's Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (part of HM Treasury) enforces asset freezes. The EU adopts sanctions that each member state enforces.
sections.title: Who imposes them

sections.text: Asset freeze (also called blocking). Nobody may pay, hold or move the target's money or property. Export controls. Sensitive goods need a licence, which is usually refused for listed buyers. Sector bans. Whole kinds of trade are cut, such as buying Russian oil above a price cap. Ownership rules. Companies owned by a listed party can be blocked without being named (section 2). Secondary sanctions (pressure on outsiders). Since Executive Order 14114 (December 2023), the US can sanction a foreign bank that handles significant deals for Russia's military industry. Foreign banks now have their own reason to check. A battlefield-goods list. The US, EU, UK and Japan share the Common High Priority List: 50 product types, by customs code, found in Russian missiles and drones. Semiconductor chips (integrated circuits) are in the top tier. Humanitarian exemptions. Since December 2022, food, medicine and aid are carved out of all UN asset freezes, and the US issues matching general licences.
sections.title: The main tools

sections.text: Governments rarely stop a shipment themselves. The list works because private gatekeepers check it and refuse: a bank will not move the money, an exporter will not sell, a shipper will not carry, an insurer will not cover. Each of them faces fines if they get it wrong. So the list is a signal. If a gatekeeper never sees the listed name, the signal never arrives. Diagram 1: the refusal chain A government lists Company A. Banks, exporters, shippers and insurers check the list and refuse Company A. Company B, the same buyer under a new name, is not on the list and passes the checks. Diagram 1. The list only works when a gatekeeper recognises the name. A new name slips through until the list catches up.
sections.title: How a sanction actually bites

sections.text: 2 · The moving parts Every sanctions case is built from the same seven pieces. Evasion means changing one piece so the others stop lining up. Goods What is traded, identified by a customs product code (codes starting 8542 are chips). Routes Which countries the paperwork says the goods left and entered. Companies The shipper, the buyer, and any middlemen. Their names are what lists match on. Ownership Who owns whom, and by how much. Decides who is blocked without being named. Lists Several, run by different governments, which do not always agree. Time When a company appeared, when it traded, and when it was finally listed. Observers Customs, banks, data companies, journalists. Each sees only part of the picture.
sections.title: What's involved

sections.text: In the US, any company owned 50% or more in total by listed parties is blocked automatically, even through a chain of other companies. Stakes from different listed owners are added together. The EU's test is slightly different: more than 50%, or "control", such as the power to appoint most of the board. The line is sharp, so where a company sits relative to it matters a lot. Diagram 2: ownership and the 50% line Example A: two listed owners hold 25% each of Company C, which adds to 50% so C is blocked. Example B: 30% known plus an unknown stake of 0 to 25% gives a range of 30 to 55%, which cannot be cleared. Diagram 2. Stakes add up toward a hard line. Solid bars are known stakes; the hatched bar is a stake we can only bound.
sections.title: The 50% rule: blocked without being named

sections.text: 3 · The tricks Almost every trick does the same thing: it breaks the match between a listed name and a transaction. Below are six, each with an example from our own work or an official source. 1. Route through a third country Goods that can no longer go straight to Russia are sold to a neighbour first, then passed on. Our data: countries' own reports to the UN show chip exports to Russia jumping from almost nothing. Kyrgyzstan: about $0 a year in 2019 to 2021, then $13.5M in 2023. Kazakhstan: $18.3M in 2022. Armenia: $13.1M in 2022. Diagram 3: third-country routing Chip makers sell to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Armenia, which pass the chips on to Russia. Each middle country's own reported chip exports to Russia rose from about zero to more than 13 million dollars. The direct route is restricted after February 2022. Diagram 3. Chip exports to Russia as each middle country itself reported them to UN Comtrade. The paperwork shows where goods were declared, not the road they took. 2. Set up front companies, then replace them New firms with no history do the trading. When one gets noticed, another takes over. Official example: the US Treasury's own entry for RM Design and Development (Kyrgyzstan) says it was established on 17 March 2022, 21 days after the invasion. The US listed it in July 2023. 3. Stay just under 50%, or hide a company in the middle A stake under the line is not blocked automatically, and an unnamed subsidiary does not show up in a name search. 4. Relabel the goods Describe a controlled item as something harmless, or file it under a different product code. Official example: in April 2026 the US Treasury described a broker shipping fentanyl ingredients labelled as "safe chemicals". 5. Transfer at sea and fly a false flag Oil is pumped from ship to ship out at sea, and tankers register under flags they are not entitled to. Official and research examples: 113 tankers under false flags carried €4.7bn of Russian oil in the first nine months of 2025. One tanker in our data changed its name five times. 6. Trade before the list catches up Listing a company takes an investigation. Until then, trading is easy. Official example: RM Design and Development was listed on 20 July 2023, at least 16 months after the founding date in its own US Treasury entry. ELEM GROUP (Kazakhstan) went on a US export blacklist in December 2023 and the US sanctions list in February 2024.
sections.title: How countries and companies evade

sections.text: 4 · The response Track the need, not the name. A name is the easiest thing to change. What Russia's weapons industry needs (a specific chip, delivered to a specific factory) changes slowly. So we watch the product, the buyer, the route, and treat company names as a lagging label.
sections.title: How we can track them

sections.text: Triangulate sources. We combine official listing pages and government releases with countries' own official trade statistics (UN Comtrade, Eurostat). A claim stands only when two independent sources agree. Comtrade is how we see the middle countries' chip exports to Russia jump after 2022. Alias and ID cross-checks. Match tax numbers and registration IDs, not just names: a name check alone misses transliterated and shortened names. Sibling finder. Look for unlisted firms sharing an address and a trading partner with a listed one. On the US list we found 240 pairs of Russia-programme companies at the same address that were listed in separate waves, a median of about 5.5 months apart. Busy addresses (registration agents, business towers) count for less. Listing-lag monitoring. Start a clock at a firm's first suspicious sign (registration, first shipment) and watch who is still trading with it after it is listed. Weapon-part tracing. Ukraine's military intelligence (GUR) publishes parts found in Russian weapons. It lists an STM32F765VIT6 microcontroller in the Shahed-136 attack drone. Searching trade records for the full part number, not the maker's name, leads from a weapon to the firms that ship that exact part. A part found in a weapon never proves that a particular shipment reached one. A built-in skeptic. A separate checker re-derives every number from the saved raw data before it is shown. It caught doubled totals (an Armenia figure of $52M that was really $13.1M) and a database start date posing as a listing date. What the data can't see Countries' own statistics show totals by country, not which companies shipped. Ship-to-ship transfers and relabelled oil. Cash deals, smuggling, and goods moved inside a country. Whether a shipped chip ended up in a weapon. Being unlisted, or absent from our data, does not mean a company is clean.
sections.title: The methods

sections.text: 5 · The stakes The parts that keep drones and missiles flying are ordinary commercial chips. Closing the gaps in Diagram 1 is how sanctions stop being paperwork. But a tool that points at companies can also hurt the wrong people, so we hold three rules.
sections.title: Why it matters, and the ethics

sections.text: A path in the data is a reason to look, not proof of wrongdoing. We only say a company is sanctioned when an official list says so. Unlisted companies our tools surface go to investigators privately, never onto a slide.
sections.title: Leads, not findings

sections.text: When gatekeepers are unsure, the cheap answer is to refuse everyone in a region. That falls on families. After US sanctions on Iran returned in 2018, medicine exports to Iran (as partner countries report them) fell by about 35%, from $1.30bn in 2017 to $0.84bn in 2023, even though medicine is meant to be exempt. Medicine exports to Russia stayed flat, about $12bn a year. In 2015 a US bank closed the accounts that carried money home to Somalia, where such transfers are 25% to 45% of the economy. Good targeting means naming the few firms that matter, not cutting off a country.
sections.title: Precision, not panic

sections.text: A false match lands on a real business: big office towers hold hundreds of companies, a few of them listed. Sharing a building is not evidence. So every lead needs two independent signals, shows its evidence rather than a score, and says what the data could not check.

sections.title: Sources

sections.text: Facts from official lists and government releases are stated as facts, with their source. Where something is our own inference (timing, shared names, one-ship companies), it is marked Lead, with a confidence note and, where it matters, an innocent explanation. How the counts were made is in METHOD.md. Counts come from public list files unless another source is named. Key to abbreviations IMO number: the seven-digit number a ship keeps for life, whatever its name. OFAC: the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, which keeps the main US sanctions list. E.O.: a US Executive Order, the legal basis for a US listing. EU act: an EU regulation published on EUR-Lex, the EU's official law site. KSE: the Kyiv School of Economics Institute, which tracks Russian oil exports monthly. CREA: the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, an advocacy research group.
sections.title: Shadow fleet: what the records show

sections.text: Fact (official list files). Of the 625 ships on the UK's Russia sanctions list, 42 are also on a US Iran-programme list when matched by IMO number. The number depends on the filter: Filter Count US entry carries an Iran programme code (strict) 42 plus Russia actions that also cite the Iran order E.O. 13846 45 plus one ship whose Iran code appears only in a second US file 46 plus ships the US listed only under its terrorism programme 54 No ship that the US listed only under its Russia programmes is inside the strict 42.

sections.text: Fact (UK dates from the UK list; US dates from OpenSanctions exports of the US list, checked against two Treasury releases). Of the strict 42, the US Iran listing came first for 30 (71%) and the UK Russia listing for 12 (29%). The median gap is 209 days. That middle value is shaped by a group of 13 ships the US listed on 30 July 2025 and the UK on 24 February 2026. The spread runs from BODHI (UK first by 477 days) to BLUEBELL (US first by 501 days). Often, but not always, the US Iran listing came first.

sections.text: Fact (official list files). 16 of the 42 hulls carry a different name on the UK list than on the US list (13 if US alternative names count). The US listed NEW MILOS on 20 March 2025; the UK listed the same IMO number as VOLANS 50 days later. JUNIA (UK) is BENEDICT (US); FIORA is GOLDEN EAGLE. The UK listed LILY on 21 July 2025; the US listed the same hull as DANYA on 29 July 2026. One hull, three identities (IMO 9282792). The UK listed CLYDE NOBLE on 9 May 2025 under an unlisted manager. Vicens Marine, a Marshall Islands company, is itself US-listed (6 February 2026, E.O. 13846). OFAC listed the hull as AQUA LIVE on 6 February 2026. The UK entry still shows the old names. (US and UK list files.) Across all sources, each hull had a median of 4 names (range 2 to 7). Ukraine's war-sanctions ship database is not a sanctions list. It shows different current names for 7 of the 42 but gives no dates, so "renamed after listing" is not shown. FIORA, UK-listed 9 May 2025, appears there under a newer name (Low).

sections.text: Fact for the counts; Lead for the "shell company" reading, which is not established. No manager of the 42 is UK-listed as a company; the UK lists the ships only. Zulu Ships Management is the only one on the EU list. About 28 companies and one individual are linked to the 42 in the US files (about 37 companies with UK-only managers). Of 18 linked companies with a set-up date in the US list file, 10 were set up in 2024 or 2025, 4 to 23 months before their ship's first listing (most 9 to 19 months). Several are named after their ship or one of its former names. Zulu Ships Management is linked to 10 of the 42 (8 via the UK manager column, 2 via OFAC links). Fleet Tanqo runs 3. On 4 IMO-confirmed pages (KAVIZ, HORAE, BRIONT, TAGOR), an entry changed on the US listing day; APATE could not be matched by IMO. For TAGOR the change was to Zulu as owner. Innocent explanation: the database may have updated its record that day. sections.text: Fact (act text on EUR-Lex). Regulation (EU) 2026/1848 of 23 July 2026 (in force 24 July) adds 41 ships (entries 652 to 692). By purpose: 27 oil, 6 stolen Ukrainian grain or cultural goods, 5 service ships, 2 energy and 1 military cargo. The service ships fall under a new rule for ships that refuel or tow listed ships: KUMANA, BILAL BEY, BEBEK-E, LADY JASMINE and OCEAN FORTUNE 18. The act gives ship-to-ship transfers as the reason. 4 of the 41 were already on the UK Russia list (PORT OLYA-3, LAURYN, SORION, LUCH). 5 are on a US Iran list. The US came first for ANAYA, BELLARIS and DAPHNE V by about 100 days, and for VIRENT by 10 days. YEHOPE was listed by the EU first and by the US 5 days later. Gaps are counted from 24 July; from 23 July, add one day. A parallel act lists 7 shipping firms: White Agate Marine (Oman), ship owner Zulu Ships Management (UAE), tanker manager Peninsular Maritime (India), technical manager Astute Maritime (Singapore), technical manager Hua Xia Shipmanagement (China), technical manager Lukoil-Marinbunker (Russia) Aquamarine Ship Management (Russia), crew recruiting Unresolved: the EUR-Lex page we read is Implementing Regulation 2026/1843; OpenSanctions cites 2026/1845. Five UAE oil traders went on an EU list in force from 13 August 2026. The UK had listed three of them (Estrella, Arcadia, Linglong) on 24 February 2026, about five months earlier.
sections.title: 6. The EU's July 2026 act

sections.text: Old ships (High). The 42 were built 1997 to 2009, counting the 37 with a build year (5 blank). KSE figures: July 2026: 150 of 268 tankers carrying Russia's seaborne oil (56%) were shadow fleet, and 93% of those were over 15 years old (via Kyiv Post, 18 September 2026). February 2026: 96% of shadow crude tankers were over 15 years old. Weak insurance (High). April 2026 (KSE): 30 shadow tankers had Russian insurers: AlfaStrakhovanie 17, Sogaz 10, Balance Insurance 3. All three insurers are listed: AlfaStrakhovanie (UK 25 November 2024, EU 18 December 2023, US), Sogaz (UK 15 March 2022, US) and JSC Balance Insurance (UK 16 June 2026). June 2026 (KSE): 48 shadow tankers had Russian insurance, 42 of them (88%) sanctioned. Spills (Medium to Low). CREA counted 50 incidents since the full-scale invasion and estimated one spill could cost coastal states $1.6 billion (2024; advocacy group). sections.text: This is the trap. The word "Iran" appears in two different ways in the US data: as a programme code on the entry (upper case, such as IRAN-EO13902 or IFSR), and as a cited order inside a Russia action (text such as "Executive Order 13846 (Iran)"). Counting the first only gives one number; counting both gives another. Adding a second US file, or the US terrorism programme, moves it again. With our files: Filter Tankers on the UK Russia list and a US list US entry carries an Iran programme code (strict) 42 plus Russia actions that also cite the Iran order E.O. 13846 (IVY, OLIA, PANDA) 45 plus a ship whose Iran code (IFSR) appears only in the Consolidated Screening List (FRUNZE) 46 plus ships the US listed only under its terrorism programme (SDGT) 54 None of the US Russia-programme ships fall inside the strict 42. Any number quoted from this work should carry its filter in the same sentence. Two teammates got 42 and 45 from the same files before we found this.
sections.title: 3. State the programme filter, every time

sections.text: Who listed first: UK date minus US date, in days. Positive means the US was first. Name mismatch: compare the UK name with the US primary name after removing spaces and punctuation. The UK list sometimes writes a ship as IMO 9417464 ('TANI'); use the quoted name. Say whether US aliases count: 16 of 42 differ on the primary name, 13 if aliases count.
sections.title: 4. Compare dates and names on the joined hulls

sections.text: A hull can carry a different name on each list, and the same name can belong to different hulls over time. Across all sources, the 42 hulls had a median of 4 names each (range 2 to 7). Search by name also returns the wrong ship. One search for a listed tanker returned a different ship with a different IMO number, which we dropped. Always confirm the IMO number on each page you use. Managers change too. Companies named after the ship they own, or after one of its former names, are common. Screening a new company name finds nothing; screening the hull finds it.
sections.title: Why names fail

sections.text: Read the UK list's "Current owner/operator" column for each joined hull and match those names against the US, EU and UK company entries after normalising (upper case, drop punctuation and suffixes such as LTD, LLC, FZE). Exact normalised matching misses spelling variants and transliterations, so "no hit" means "not found by this matcher", not "proven unlisted". Registered-agent addresses are noise. One Majuro address had about 145 rows in the US file; a Seychelles address had 16 rows across unrelated programmes. Treat an address shared by more than about 15 listed firms as an agent's address, not a cluster. Publishing rule: tools/fleet/mgrs.py replaces the name of any manager with no list hit by UNLISTED-nn. Keep it that way for anything public.

sections.text: A tanker has a seven-digit IMO number that is stamped on the hull and stays with it for life. Its name, flag, owner and manager can all change. Many of them go by different names on the two lists, and most are run by small, recently created companies that manage one ship each. Following the name loses the ship; following the hull number keeps it.

sections.text: Join by IMO number (build_base.py). Every ship on the UK Russia list, the EU ship list, or the US list under an Iran, Russia, terrorism or Venezuela programme becomes one node keyed IMO<number>. Yachts and passenger ships are dropped. Names from each list and former names from Ukraine's database are kept on the node. Lines from the lists. UK "current owner/operator" -> operates; OFAC "Linked To" -> linked to; OFAC registered owner -> owns; flags and former flags -> flagged in / was flagged in; each listing -> sanctioned by, with its date. Company matching. Names are normalised (case, punctuation, legal suffixes such as LLC, DMCC, FZE, PJSC). The research and verification files stay with the team's working files and are not published, because they name unlisted firms. Only the corrected files feed the chart. sections.text: A sanctions list only works when someone recognises the name. After Russia's full invasion of Ukraine (24 Feb 2022), Western chips kept reaching Russia through new countries (Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, the UAE, Armenia, Turkey) and short-lived companies. sections.text: Every night the shadow-fleet map and the influence network are rebuilt from the official sanctions lists and US lobbying filings. This page lists what each rebuild added, removed or changed, newest day first. Each change links to the graph that shows it.
sections.title: What changed, day by day

sections.text: Trace the Unseen, Sanctions track, 25 September 2026. Two research waves (16 researchers), each report checked by an independent verifier who re-opened the filings and sources. Corrections from the verifiers are applied below. How to read this. Lobbying is legal. We state what official records show (lobbying disclosures, foreign-agent filings, Treasury notices, votes, court rulings) plainly, with the source. For effects, every claim carries a grade: Documented influence: an official record, ruling or statement ties the outcome to the lobbying or to a named actor's position. Timing fits: the lobbying came before the change, but no record ties them together. Contested: other explanations (diplomacy, security reviews, courts, markets, party politics) are at least as strong. Timing is never treated as proof. Sources we used first: US Lobbying Disclosure Act filings (the Senate's public API, lda.senate.gov), US foreign-agent (FARA) filings (efile.fara.gov), the Federal Register, US Treasury and Commerce releases, EU law (EUR-Lex) and EU court rulings, congressional votes. Press and think tanks come second and are labelled.
sections.title: Lobbying around sanctions: who pays, through whom, and what changed

sections.text: The pattern: the companies that evade don't lobby; the money moves through respectable names. None of these has a single US lobbying filing under its own name: RM Design and Development, ELEM Group, Keremet Bank, Zulu Ships Management, Fleet Tanqo, Sovcomflot, Lukoil, Rosneft, Nayara Energy, Litasco, Megasan (checked in the Senate lobbying database). Evasion uses new names; lobbying uses respectable ones: a parent company, a US subsidiary, a law firm, or a government. Case The clean name on the record What the record shows Rusal (US-sanctioned 2018, removed 2019) Its parent, En+ Group Rusal: 0 lobbying filings. En+ hired Mercury Public Affairs under FARA (registration 6170) at $108,500 a month from 2019 (cut to $54,250 from January 2020), and DCI Group under the lobbying law ($10,000 rising to $40,000 a quarter; issues: low-carbon aluminium, aluminium tariffs), filings through at least early 2025. Hikvision (on US Commerce's Entity List) Its US subsidiary, Hikvision USA Lobbying through Sidley Austin, rising from $140,000 (Q2 2018) to $500,000 a quarter (Q2 2019 to Q1 2021), on export controls, foreign relations, homeland security. SMIC (Entity List) A law firm The filing's client field reads "Akin Gump on behalf of Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation", with a second firm working under Akin Gump. Hytera (Entity List) A law firm Lobbying filings through Duane Morris (amounts not re-checked). Semiconductor chip makers Their own names NVIDIA, AMD, Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Arrow and the Semiconductor Industry Association lobby openly on export controls. NVIDIA spent $940,000 in-house in Q1 2025 on "export controls including implementation of P.L. 115-232" (filing ded7018b). The industry association spends $500,000 a quarter in-house, plus a firm filing under "Trade Sanctions". Getting off a list Law firms registered as foreign agents US law firms register under FARA to seek removal from US sanctions lists for Russia-programme clients (for example registration 7554, 2025; the client's name is blacked out). Kazakhstan's state oil company, sovereign fund and embassy A lobbying firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck (FARA 5870): $579,900 for the six months to August 2024. No sanctions wording found in the filings we read. Lukoil's Bulgarian refinery A government Bulgaria won the EU's only exemption to import Russian crude by sea, for the Lukoil-owned Burgas refinery. Its finance ministry denied lobbying for Lukoil (Politico). Also found: Russian-linked entities are suspended from the EU Transparency Register (Politico), so they can't lobby EU institutions directly. None of Alrosa, Norilsk Nickel, Belaruskali or Belarusian Potash has a current US, EU or UK register filing.
sections.title: Part 1. Who lobbies, and through whom

sections.text: Main result: no case shows documented causation from a lobbying payment to a sanctions outcome. The strongest documented influence comes from governments protecting their own industries, and it opened exactly the gap the shadow fleet now fills.
sections.title: Part 2. Did it change anything?

sections.text: In 2022 Greek, Maltese and Cypriot shipowners and their governments turned the EU's proposed ban on shipping Russian oil into the G7 price cap, set near the market price. In 2025 and 2026, Greece and Malta are still blocking a full EU ban on maritime services (documented government positions). The shadow fleet became the main channel for Russian oil. Russia's oil revenue was $13.5 billion in August 2025 (down $0.9 billion). Grade: documented for the governments' current positions; timing fits for 2022.
sections.title: Shipping and the oil price cap

sections.text: Pipeline oil to Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia (Druzhba), Bulgaria's Burgas exemption, and nickel, palladium and aluminium left off EU lists kept Russian trade flowing for years. These came from government-to-government negotiation, not registered lobbying. The delay of the EU ban on Russian diamonds (Antwerp, Alrosa): industry lobbying is reported by the press only. Grade: contested.
sections.title: EU carve-outs

sections.text: 6 April 2018: OFAC listed Oleg Deripaska, En+, Rusal and EuroSibEnergo. 19 December 2018 OFAC told Congress it would remove the companies after a restructuring (the "Barker Plan": an independent chair, reduced voting power for Deripaska). 16 January 2019: Mercury (for En+) filed a paper titled "How the Barker Plan Permanently Removes Oleg Deripaska" with the Justice Department; the same day the Senate voted 57 to 42 on blocking the removal (60 needed), so the block failed. Deripaska himself stayed on the US list, and the EU listed him on 8 April 2022. Grade: timing fits (downgraded by the verifier from "documented"). Contested: Treasury negotiated the deal, and the vote split largely along party lines.
sections.title: Rusal's removal from the US list

sections.text: Across 2025's back-and-forth (a licence requirement for NVIDIA's H20 in April, the AI Diffusion rule withdrawn on 13 May, H20 licences from August, H200 moved to case-by-case review in January 2026), NVIDIA's in-house lobbying went $940,000 -> $620,000 -> $1.95 million -> $1.46 million a quarter, and AMD's ran $1.1 to 1.7 million. Outcome: NVIDIA took a $4.5 billion H20 write-off and reported only about $50 million of H20 revenue after the licences (Q3 fiscal 2026). A charged smuggling scheme (Southern District of New York) sent about $510 million of servers to China, part of a $2.5 billion total. Grade: timing fits; documented influence thin.
sections.title: AI chip export rules

sections.text: The Chip Security Act (location checks for AI chips, S.1705 / H.R.3447, May 2025) has not moved out of committee while industry lobbying rose. The Commerce Department (BIS) is asking Congress for its largest-ever enforcement staffing increase (FY2027 request), and US designations fell sharply from their 2024 peak. Grade: timing only; a policy shift is the other explanation.
sections.title: Enforcement capacity

sections.text: The US removes firms from its Russia list routinely with no visible paid lobbying (for example Sberbank's Kazakh subsidiary, removed 8 March 2023 after it was sold). EU courts annul a real share of Russia listings on evidence grounds (documented in the rulings). Removal rarely means trade resumes: other lists still apply. Megasan came off the main US list on 29 June 2026 (Federal Register 2026-18610) and is still on the Commerce Entity List; no lobbying or foreign-agent filing exists under its name.
sections.title: Getting off lists

sections.text: Licences for US suppliers followed the Commerce Department's licensing policy; no documented link to Hikvision's or SMIC's lobbying was found.
sections.title: Chinese listed firms

sections.text: Studies show lobbying on sanctions happens and goes with access (for example the "Lobbying EU Sanctions" business survey; Kim and Milner on business and foreign policy). None measures the effect on outcomes causally. Journalism quantifies the money and the revolving door better than the studies quantify impact.
sections.title: What research says

sections.text: "The biggest hole in the oil sanctions wasn't bought by a lobbyist. It was negotiated by EU governments protecting their shipping industries, and the shadow fleet grew into it." And: "Rusal never filed a lobbying disclosure. Its parent did, for $108,500 a month."

sections.text: EU and UK lobbying registers were only lightly searched; Russian-linked entities are barred from the EU register. Two figures are unchecked: Sidley Austin's parallel foreign-agent total for Hikvision, and Hytera's amounts. Several FARA exhibits black out the client's name. Lobbying outside the US disclosure systems (in Brussels, national capitals, or through think tanks and associations) is mostly invisible in public records. The trace of listed companies lobbying through clean intermediaries is in clean-names-graph/: an interactive graph of 63 organisations and 63 links (51 documented).

sections.title: Clean names, listed interests

sections.text: A listed company rarely signs a lobbying form itself. A clean name signs instead, and the listed company appears only in the small print: A US subsidiary as the client: Hikvision USA, Huawei Technologies USA, Futurewei, Sberbank CIB USA. A parent as the client: En+ Group for Rusal. A law firm "on behalf of": "Akin Gump on behalf of SMIC". A funded project company: Nord Stream 2 AG for Gazprom. A trade association or coalition: drone coalitions funded by DJI; the US-China Business Council. A government: Bulgaria for Lukoil's Burgas refinery; Russian ministries for state banks. US lobbying filings have a "foreign entities" box where the client must name foreign companies that own, control or fund it. That box is where many listed parents appear: Hangzhou Hikvision and its state-owned parent CETC behind Hikvision USA (2022), and Huawei behind Huawei Technologies USA and Futurewei (2022). Lobbying is legal. Being listed is a legal status; nothing here says any lobbying was unlawful.
sections.title: The pattern

sections.text: 61 organisations: 17 listed companies, 12 clean intermediaries, 6 trade associations or coalitions, 20 lobbying or law firms, 6 governments or lawmakers. 60 links: 48 Documented (an official record shows the link) and 12 Leads (plausible, not yet proven, drawn dashed). 228 lobbying filings with foreign entities from Russia, Belarus, Iran, China, Hong Kong, the UAE, Turkey or Kazakhstan were scanned, and 616 names checked against the lists. Most pre-2022 hits (Alfa-Bank, Gazprom, VEB) came years before those firms were listed, so they show the channel, not lobbying while listed.
sections.title: By the numbers

sections.text: Hikvision (on the US export blacklist since 9 Oct 2019). Its US arm, Hikvision USA, paid Sidley Austin up to $500,000 a quarter (2018 to 2021). A 2022 filing through The Elevation Association names Hangzhou Hikvision and state-owned CETC as foreign entities. Documented. Rusal via En+. Rusal filed nothing under its own name. Its parent En+ paid Mercury Public Affairs $108,500 a month (later $54,250) from 2019 to 2022 under the foreign-agent law, and DCI Group $10,000 to $40,000 a quarter from 2021 to 2025. The hiring is documented; the ownership link as drawn is a lead. SMIC (on the US export blacklist). "Akin Gump on behalf of SMIC" reported $50,000 to $140,000 a quarter (2020 to 2022) on export eligibility; Capitol Counsel also named SMIC as a foreign entity. Documented. Sberbank. Its US arm, Sberbank CIB USA, paid the Madison Group ($50,000 to $105,000) and the Podesta Group ($20,000 to $110,000) a quarter in 2016 and 2017. Documented. Gazprom via Nord Stream 2. Capitol Counsel and Roberti Global lobbied on pipeline permitting (Q3 2017). The filings themselves say Gazprom funds 50% of the pipeline company and the Russian state owns 38% of Gazprom. Documented. Also on the graph: Huawei through Huawei Technologies USA (Squire Patton Boggs) and Futurewei; DJI as a funder of drone coalitions (its US arm's link to the listed parent is a lead); Arctic LNG 2, which is itself listed and filed directly, the reverse pattern; Lukoil through the government of Bulgaria; Alrosa and the Antwerp World Diamond Centre (a lead, from press reporting).

sections.title: Sanctions Influence Network

sections.text: The front companies don't lobby; their owners do. As of 25 September 2026 we found zero US lobbying reports for the 18 ship managers, front companies and oil traders we searched, including Sovcomflot, Zulu, Fleet Tanqo, Lukoil and Rosneft. The lobbying comes from parent companies, banks and state-linked firms. Nord Stream 2 paid Washington firms $13.87 million (2016 to 2022) (as of 25 September 2026), much of it on Russia-sanctions legislation such as S.722. The total is counted once per firm, client and quarter, with amendments and subcontracts not double-counted, and was checked by hand. Sanctioned Russian banks lobbied on the scope of sanctions. Sberbank's US arm, VTB and Gazprombank hired firms after 2014; one stated issue was "clarifying scope of sanctions imposed by Executive Order 13660". All three are fully blocked (as of 25 September 2026). Only 14 records join the two sides (as of 25 September 2026). Examples: the Russian state owns Sovcomflot (Treasury); Gazprom owns Gazprom Neft, whose subsidiary runs listed tankers (Treasury); Rosneft controls its tanker company Rosnefteflot (Treasury); the US list, as of 25 September 2026, links seven shipping companies to Arctic LNG 2, which hired a Washington firm in 2023. The revolving door is on the record. {{stat:kg.lobbyists_with_posts}} lobbyists on these accounts disclose past government posts, including former senators and a former counselor to the Secretary of the Treasury. Some listed ships are sailing right now. Of 27 listed ships broadcasting positions in our God's Eye snapshot of 25 September 2026, 24 are on the map; six connect through state-owned Sovcomflot to the lobbying side.

sections.title: Method in brief

sections.text: Documented ({{stat:kg.documented_edges}} links): an official record states it directly. Reported ({{stat:kg.reported_edges}}): an official filing seen in summary only. Lead ({{stat:kg.lead_edges}}): our inference, drawn dotted, hideable with the Leads filter. We describe documented conduct with its source and make no legal findings; "charged" is never "convicted". People are named only where an official list or release names them, or in their own lobbying disclosure, in that role. Unlisted firms known only from non-official sources appear as a description (12 as of 25 September 2026).
sections.title: Confidence and naming

sections.text: "No path found" and "no lobbying found" are not proof of no relationship or no influence. US lobbying only, plus a few EU register entries from team research; fees are self-reported and rounded to $10,000. En+ Group cannot be searched by name on the lobbying API (the "+" is ignored); it comes from earlier targeted pulls. Bills are limited to key bills and those named in three or more reports ({{stat:kg.bills}}). Live AIS is a moment in time: sanctioned tankers often switch off or spoof their transponders. This page explains, in plain terms, where every piece came from, how we joined them, and how sure we are. sections.title: Methods and sources.

sections.text: Every ship, company and person on the map comes from a government list or a public filing. We did not add anyone from news stories or guesswork. Every line on the map has a source you can open: click any dot, and each connection shows the record it came from. Lines we inferred ourselves are drawn dotted and labelled "lead". There are {{stat:kg.lead_edges}} of them out of {{stat:kg.edges}} lines, and you can switch them off. The main finding is also a limit: the front companies that run the ships never appear in US lobbying records. Their parent companies, banks and state owners do. Only 14 records connect the two (as of 25 September 2026).
sections.title: The short version

sections.text: Source What we used it for UK sanctions list report of 21 Sep 2026 for the research, then refreshed nightly Ships the UK has banned, with their hull numbers, current owners or operators, and past flags. gov.uk US sanctions and export lists The US Treasury's list of blocked people and companies (the "SDN" list, short for Specially Designated Nationals), plus the US government's combined screening list, which adds lighter restrictions: limits on certain loans and investments, the list of Chinese military companies, and the Commerce Department's export blacklist (the "Entity List"). US ship entries say which company each ship is "linked to". trade.gov EU asset-freeze list and ship bans Which companies and people the European Union has frozen (asset freezes, Regulation 269/2014), and which ships it bans from its ports and services (Regulation 833/2014), with the dates. Ukraine's war-sanctions database Former names and flags of ships. It is a research database kept by Ukraine, not a sanctions list, and we never use it to say something is sanctioned. US lobbying reports Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act, every paid lobbyist in Washington files public reports each quarter: who hired them, how much they were paid, which bills and agencies they worked on, and any government jobs the lobbyists held before. We downloaded every page of reports for the companies in our story from the official database. lda.gov API Foreign-agent filings People who lobby for foreign clients also register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act ("FARA"). We used two of these filings, for En+ Group (the aluminium and energy group in which, its lobbying report states, Oleg Deripaska held 35% of the voting rights) and Hikvision. En+ Group exhibit, Hikvision statement US Treasury press releases Official statements about who owns whom, for example "Gazprom Neft is majority owned by Gazprom" (release jl2629, 2014) and "Sovcomflot, Russia's state-owned shipping company" (release jy2777, 2025). The VeilTrace team's shadow-fleet map The ship and company layer, built by a VeilTrace team member from the lists above and joined by hull number. We use its output as is and follow its rules. The VeilTrace team's lobbying research A VeilTrace team member's separate study of lobbying around sanctions, including Europe's lobbying register (for example the Antwerp diamond centre arguing against a diamond ban, and Russian firms' Brussels consultants) and ownership links such as Rosneft's control of its tanker company Rosnefteflot. Where it names the same organisation as ours, the two were merged into one dot; its 32 extra links (as of 25 September 2026) keep their own sources and labels. God's Eye View (our sanctions layer) Our add-on to an open-source 3D globe that matches listed ships to live ship-tracking signals (AIS, the Automatic Identification System that ships broadcast). A snapshot taken at 20:11 UTC on 25 Sep 2026 found 27 listed ships broadcasting; 24 of them are on this map and pulse green.
sections.title: Where the data comes from

sections.text: Start with the ships. A ship's name can change with paperwork, but its hull number, issued by the International Maritime Organization (the "IMO number"), stays with it for life. We join every list by that number, so one ship with five names is still one dot. Attach the companies. The lists say who owns, manages or operates each ship. Those become the lines between ships and companies. {{stat:kg.ships_hidden}} listed ships have no owner or operator named on any list, so they are not drawn. Choose the lobbying clients. We picked the companies in our story: Russian banks and energy firms such as Sberbank, VTB, Gazprombank, Gazprom, Nord Stream 2, Novatek and Arctic LNG 2; Chinese firms on US blacklists such as Huawei, ZTE, SMIC, Hikvision and DJI; and the US semiconductor industry's trade group and Nvidia. We also searched for the shipping companies themselves. Read every report. We pulled all pages of lobbying reports for those names ({{stat:kg.filings_scanned}} reports) and kept the {{stat:kg.filings_kept}} whose client really is one of them. Name searches catch look-alikes, such as "ZTEK Corp" for ZTE or turkey farmers for Turkey, so every client is matched against an exact list. Count the money once. Lobbying firms often correct a quarter's report, and the corrected version repeats the same fee. We count each firm, client and quarter once, using the latest version that states an amount. When a firm hires a subcontractor, the subcontractor also reports that money; we show that link but do not add it to the client's total, because it is already inside the main firm's fee. We checked one total by hand: Nord Stream 2 paid its Washington firms $13.87 million from 2016 to 2022 (as of 25 September 2026). Before this cleanup the same data added up to $18.9 million. Look up sanctions status by record number. For every lobbying client we found its exact entry on the US and UK lists and recorded the entry number. A solid red ring means a government blocked it, which is an asset freeze (a US SDN entry, a UK asset freeze or EU Regulation 269/2014). A dashed ring means it is restricted: limits on trade, ports or investment, such as the UK and EU bans that keep a listed ship out of their ports and services, but not an asset freeze. Gazprom, for example, is restricted, not blocked. Connect the two sides only with official records. We hand-checked each link between the lobbying side and the fleet against a government source: Treasury's statements of who owns whom, and US list entries that link seven shipping companies to Arctic LNG 2 (as of 25 September 2026). Each one shows its source when you click it. Merge the VeilTrace team's work. A VeilTrace team member's lobbying study and our layer named many of the same organisations. We matched them by name, checked every match by hand (as of 25 September 2026, four look-alikes were kept apart, such as Nord Stream AG and Nord Stream 2), and kept one dot per organisation. When both had a link between the same pair, we kept ours because it carries the filing number and amount. Record the revolving door. Lobbyists must list the government jobs they held before. We took those words exactly as each lobbyist wrote them, which gives {{stat:kg.lobbyists_with_posts}} lobbyists with past posts, from former senators to a former counselor to the Secretary of the Treasury.
sections.title: How we built it

sections.text: Every line carries one of three labels. Documented An official record says it directly: a sanctions list, a government press release, or the lobbying report itself. {{stat:kg.documented_edges}} lines. Reported From an official filing we saw summarised but did not re-open ourselves. Lines of this kind: {{stat:kg.reported_edges}}. Lead Our own inference, for example that "Gazprom Flot" belongs to Gazprom because of its name. A lead is a reason to look closer, not a finding. {{stat:kg.lead_edges}} lines, drawn dotted, and the "Leads" switch hides them. We describe what records show, in plain words, with the source attached. We do not say anyone broke the law unless a court or government agency has said so. A person who has been charged is "charged", not "convicted".
sections.title: How sure we are

sections.text: People are named only when a government list or official release names them, in that role, or when they are lobbyists named in their own public lobbying reports. As of 25 September 2026, six people from the shadow-fleet research have not yet had their official source re-checked; they are marked "(?)". Unlisted companies known only from non-official sources are not named. They appear as a description, such as "unlisted India ship manager" (27 of them, as of 25 September 2026). This follows the VeilTrace team's rule for the shadow-fleet map. Hollow shapes are companies that run listed ships but are on no list themselves (375, as of 25 September 2026). That is a fact about the lists, not an accusation.
sections.title: Who we name, and who we don't

sections.text: "No connection found" is not "no connection." The map only knows what is written in the records we used. The path finder says so when it finds nothing. No lobbying report does not mean no influence. Influence can also run through foreign-agent filings, European lobbying, embassies or governments. On 25 September 2026 we searched 18 ship managers, front companies and oil traders and found zero US lobbying reports for any of them. Lobbying fees are approximate. The law lets firms round their income to the nearest $10,000, and totals are what firms reported, not what we audited. Only US lobbying. We did not add Europe's lobbying register or trade-association member lists yet. Some searches were impossible. The lobbying database ignores the "+" in "En+ Group", so En+ comes only from an earlier, narrower search. Bills are filtered. We show the key bills named in our story and any bill named in three or more reports ({{stat:kg.bills}} in total), to keep the picture readable. "Live" is a moment, not a record. The green pulse means a ship's transponder was seen at the time of the snapshot. Sanctioned tankers often switch transponders off or broadcast false positions, so a ship without the pulse may still be at sea. Part of it is a snapshot. Lists change every week. The ships, companies, lobbying reports and counts above are rebuilt every night from the official lists and lobbying filings (latest build {{stat:generated}}). The hand-checked links and every figure marked "as of 25 September 2026" come from the research of that day and are not rebuilt.
sections.title: What the map cannot tell you

sections.text: Click any dot on the map: the side panel lists every connection with its date, record number and a source link to the official page or filing. The raw lobbying reports we downloaded are kept with the date and time of each download. The scripts that rebuild the map from those files sit next to it in scripts/. This map was built on the day of the event by the VeilTrace team working with AI agents (Claude Code) that did research, cross-checking and building under human direction. Every number above was re-derived from the saved records, and the corrections that checking forced (such as the double-counted lobbying fees) are described on this page.
